newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi coffee sold despite regional trade embargo.
newsitem.headline: Burundi coffee sold despite regional trade embargo.

text.p: Burundi has sold most of its 1996/97 coffee crop despite a trade embargo imposed on the country by regional leaders since last July, officials said on Wednesday.
Sales are expected to continue.

Thomas Minani, general manager of the Burundi Coffee Office (Ocibu), the government body responsible for the sector, said about 14,000 tonnes of mild arabicas had been sold and contracts had been signed for another 2,800 tonnes.

Ocibu figures put total arabica production for 1996/97 at 25,000 tonnes. Minani said Ocibu would try to sell the balance of around 8,200 tonnes by auction in the capital Bujumbura and expected sales to be completed by June.
Unofficial figures obtained from Ocibu showed that as much as 17,190 tonnes had been sold so far, of which 15,048 were fully washed arabicas.
Minani said production in 1995/96 was also about 25,000 tonnes and forecast an increase for the 1997/98 crop, which is being harvested now.
"For the next crop we are expecting a bit more in terms of production -- about 27,000 tonnes," Minani said.
"We (also) expect quality to improve because we now have enough insecticide," he said.
Officials and exporters blame declines in yield and quality in 1996/97 on the civil war and the embargo.
Charles Ntezahorigwa, managing director of a leading coffee house, said Burundi's crop would normally average 32,000 tonnes.
He said quality for previous crop years was lower than normal because farmers were not always able to apply inputs such as pesticide on a regular basis.

Ocibu officials said insecticide for the 1997/98 crop had been imported directly from Europe. Ntezahorigwa said rains were good last year but "the blockade delayed processing so the 1996/97 crop is a bit oldish."

Exporters said the primary obstacle they faced was the embargo. Economic and transport sanctions were imposed on Burundi by regional leaders in response to a coup last July that installed Pierre Buyoya.
Before that most of Burundi's coffee was exported via Dar es Salaam in Tanzania.

The embargo was eased last month at a regional summit in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha, allowing free movement of medicine, food, agricultural products and education and construction materials in and out of the country.

Despite that, Burundi's borders remain closed to commercial traffic. Officials at Ocibu told Reuters that coffee was not included in a list published in Dar es Salaam last week of goods approved for shipment through Tanzania.
"The embargo is not yet over, especially for coffee. We shall have to wait and see," Minani said. "If in July we can send our coffee freely (through Tanzania) it will be very good for us."
Ntezahorigwa said his company exported no coffee last year but described the mood among coffee exporters as "optimistic".
The Burundi Coffee Co said they expected to start exports in the coming season after a year of no sales. "I think we can be optimistic about next year's crop," an official told Reuters.
Regardless of whether the embargo was lifted or not, Minani said coffee sales would continue.
Witnesses at Bujumbura airport said sacks of coffee have been stacked high on the tarmac in recent months.

Commercial pilots say the coffee is routed through Angola and South Africa to final destinations in Europe. Minani said some planes "are going straight to Europe where primary markets exist in Germany and Scandinavia."
Coffee has traditionally accounted for more than 80 percent of the country's foreign currency receipts.
